title: The Taylor Swift fandom is changing | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

When Zachary Hourihane met Taylor Swift at the age of 17, he cried so hard he stained her dress.

“It was like a sensory overload,” he said. “It was really like when you bring a 5 year old to Disney World and you think it’s gonna be the best day of their life, but they cry the whole time.”

Hourihane, now 30, went on to build a career on social media as “The Swiftologist,” releasing video essays on YouTube and TikTok as well as co-hosting the “Evolution of a Snake: The Taylor Swift Fan Podcast” with fellow Swiftie Madeline Rubicam, whom he met when they were teens. He mixed in a bit of criticism on his journey to becoming one of Swift’s biggest fans. Is Swift an “ethical billionaire?” Hourihane doesn’t believe such a thing exists and shared that opinion in 2023.

But recently, Hourihane’s critiques have felt more pointed, with an increased willingness to publicly highlight not just the hits, but the misses from the woman responsible for his social media moniker. That was especially true following the release of Swift’s 2025 album, “The Life of a Showgirl” — a project for which shescored Grammy nominationsthis week, including best album — and the additional tracks she released in September. Swift is still riding high — on Wednesday, she is set to perform at the Country Music Association Awards for the first time in 13 years — but for some fans, their relationship to her is changing.

“I still love Taylor and I still deeply appreciate what she has brought to my life, but also I think I am able to deprogram that kind of stan brain where it has to be an obsessive and compulsive devotion to her,” Hourihane said in an interview from Singapore, where he lives. “And the more pushback I get from the Swifties, the more I’m like, ‘I’m doing the right thing. I’m making strides where they need to happen.’”

Following years of blind adoration of Swift, Hourihane has become a proxy for those willing to be more critical of the star when they feel she’s missed the mark. It feels in keeping with the times in which we live, where, from pop culture to politics, people seem more resistant to blindly supporting their favorites.

“I think that the ultimate love, the ultimate act of love is critique. When you really love a piece of art, you want it to be better,” he said. “And I think that criticism is a public good. It creates this third space where we demand more of artists and ourselves.”

Hourihane first came to adore Swift after watching her perform her 2006 song “Our Story” on MTV.

“She was twirling around on this porch, on this set that seemed very American to me,” he recalled. “And there was something about America — the idea of America — that came through very clearly with those early Taylor Swift songs.”

As a young gay child, he said, he found hope in how Swift was able to freely express herself.

“Taylor Swift seemed to live in this place that was very open to having a young girl tell her own story and be the master of her own destiny and be able to right wrongs that were done onto her,” he said. “She could write songs about it. She could literally take control of the bad things that happened to her by narrativizing it and that was deeply inspirational to me as someone that was withholding a lot.”

By the time he watched her performance of “Love Story” at the 2008 CMA Awards, Hourihane was ready to seek out his people.

“That was a moment that I felt compelled to go on the internet and look up and re-watch the video and through that I kind of discovered like fan forums and eventually Tumblr, places where I would get to commune with other people who felt the way that I did about Taylor Swift, which was an immense and incredible fixation on wanting to know everything,” he said.

The Swiftologist began to take shape as he immersed himself in the Swifteverse and her devout fanbase: the Swifties.

He won a chance to meet her at a meet and greet in Singapore in 2013. After he stained her dress with his tears, he recalled that Swift said “I didn’t even like that dress anyway.” He was enchanted.

He met the star again two years later after a show in Dublin — something arranged he said by her mother, who recognized what a huge fan he was following his first meeting with her. In 2017, he achieved what “is like summiting Everest as a Swiftie” when the superstar invited him to her home for a listening party for some new music.

He took his background having been a young journalist reviewing concerts and writing about pop culture for local blogs and publications and married it to his obsession with Swift to become The Swiftologist. Since posting his first video on YouTube in 2020, he garnered more than half a million followers on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram combined.

He and Rubicam had launched their podcast the year before, intent on using their super fandom as an opportunity to dissect and discuss Swift’s music and career. Since then, he has continued to lean into that fandom as much as the criticism and even attended 13 Eras Tour concerts.

It was reading the works of the late American film critic Pauline Kael, and journalists Janet Malcolm and Joan Didion that put Hourihane on the path to being more critical, he said.

“The Silent Woman: Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes,” Malcolm’s book on the poets and the very nature of biography, had a particularly profound effect on Hourihane.

He found the book to be “really confrontational” and said it “deconstructs a lot of the myths” about the famed author.

“And Sylvia Plath and Taylor Swift, actually, there is an interesting relationship between those two cultural figures and how women identify with them specifically,” he said.

While reading the book, he said he “was just so astounded by the level of thinking, and I had this instinctive response where I was like, ‘You’re wrong. I don’t like what you’re saying.’”

“But when I read her argument, I couldn’t fault any of her logic,” he said. “And there were obviously things I didn’t like about what she said, but I really understood the value of having that perspective articulated so well.

Reading that book put him on the path of realization that he could think about Swift and his fandom differently, he said.

Critical thinking does not mean he’s turned against the woman that has meant so much to him and who he still believes “is the greatest living songwriter.”

“I believe that even when she’s releasing work that I don’t think is perhaps up to her own standards, I think that she has this incredible capacious imagination and a really distinct ability to make the personal universal, which is like one of the most sacred writing rules,” he said.

When Swift is at her best, he said, “she is rendering very intimate, special, personal moments in a way that feels as though they could apply to you,” even “a gay boy growing up in Singapore.”

“Like that is the power of Taylor Swift and her understanding of human emotion. I think she really is a chronicler of the heart.”
